text:
**Yes, a 20,000 mAh power bank is allowed on a US flight, in your carry-on only.**

**Why it's under the limit:** The FAA caps spare lithium-ion batteries and power banks at 100 Wh each. To convert, divide mAh by 1000 and multiply by the voltage. A typical power bank is rated at 3.7 V, so 20,000 mAh is 20 Ah × 3.7 V ≈ 74 Wh. The FAA explains the calculation [here](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/airline-passengers-and-batteries). Check the Wh printed on your bank, since some are labeled directly.

**Rules to follow:**
- **Carry-on only.** Power banks are prohibited in checked bags ([FAA](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/more_info/?hazmat=7)).
- **If your carry-on gets gate-checked,** take the power bank out and keep it with you in the cabin.
- **Protect the terminals.** Leave it in retail packaging, tape over the ports, or use a pouch or case so it can't short-circuit.
- **Don't bring a damaged or recalled bank.**
- **Check your airline's policy.** Many airlines limit how many power banks you can carry, regardless of capacity. The FAA says to check with your carrier ([FAA](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/airline-passengers-and-batteries)). The [IATA](https://www.iata.org/en/youandiata/travelers/batteries/) guidance says the same.

**Larger banks:** Anything from 101 to 160 Wh needs airline approval, with a limit of two per person. Above 160 Wh is not allowed on passenger aircraft.
